A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COM4D and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across the expanded and renumbered appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction benchmarks, component ablations, a user-preference study, and CMU Panoptic evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds synthetic-scene evaluation, mesh-interpenetration measurements, a Shape of Motion comparison, and qualitative tests.

M1.justification: Attention Parsing, Attention Mixing, the 21-block DiT, diffusion forcing, losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged. The new statement about supporting 16 parts with additional fine-tuning does not document an architectural or algorithmic revision.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks and generated-video examples, v2 evaluates a newly constructed synthetic compositional 4D dataset with reference static and dynamic geometry (Supplementary Sections I–J). Section F also adds a moving-camera scenario involving dynamic objects, extending the previously fixed-camera evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Supplementary Section H adds an evaluated optimization-based comparator, Shape of Motion (SOM), for compositional reconstruction. The original MIDI, PartCrafter, TripoSG, V2M4, GVFD, L4GM, and internal-ablation comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Existing training and evaluation settings are retained. New protocols include separate static-scene and dynamic-object scoring on synthetic compositions, averaging dynamic scores within samples before averaging across samples, and measuring mesh-intersection IoU across eight videos. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The original embedding, diffusion-forcing, and attention-mixing ablations remain unchanged. v2 adds targeted checks of physical interpenetration and qualitative moving-camera and interaction cases in Supplementary Sections F–G; these provide limited additional robustness evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing mean-score and user-preference reporting is retained; the new metric aggregation rules concern evaluation design rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the existing Panoptic and user-study values are unchanged. v2 adds synthetic static CD/F-score of 0.293/0.418 and dynamic scores of 0.284/0.434 (Table 4), interaction IoU of 0.0096, and SOM CD of 11.30 cm alongside COM4D’s retained 7.42 cm. New object-count statistics and qualitative examples also expand the reported findings.

T1.justification: The formal problem formulation, attention equations, and training losses, including supplementary Equations 4–5, are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical definition is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: compositional 4D reconstruction through separately learned spatial and temporal attention, without compositional 4D training data, and strong performance on the constituent reconstruction tasks.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and limitation discussions. It describes degradation with increasing object count, qualifies the camera restriction for dynamic-only scenes, interprets low mesh overlap as evidence of implicit physical plausibility, and attributes weaker synthetic-scene scores to accumulated object-placement errors. These extend v1’s discussion of occlusion, physical causality, and fixed cameras.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a promised release to reported availability at the same repository. Supplementary Section I adds synthetic-data construction, normalization, asset-transformation, GLB-export, metadata, and rendering details; Section D mentions additional fine-tuning for 16 parts. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 99 works and the main related-work discussion is unchanged. New Supplementary Section H specifically contrasts COM4D’s learned generative priors with the already-cited SOM’s incomplete or noisy reconstructions under occlusion.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains nearly verbatim, with small wording edits and an added pointer to synthetic evaluation. The supplement inserts new topical sections around retained material, but does not extensively rewrite or reorganize the existing argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 13–18 and Table 4 for moving-camera, interaction, SOM, and synthetic-scene evidence. Earlier Figures 13–16 are retained as Figures 19–22 and reflowed across the appendix. These additions and relocations substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The synthetic component-level evaluation and SOM comparison strengthen evidence for the central compositional task beyond v1’s attention-mixing comparisons, while the placement-error and applicability discussions clarify limitations. The gains remain limited by the unspecified synthetic test-set size, sparse SOM evaluation details, and narrow physical-plausibility and moving-camera checks.
